title: A Major Trial Put Keto Against the Mediterranean Diet. Keto Won.
description: What’s healthier for your heart and liver: bacon and eggs, or oatmeal and quinoa? It seems like a bizarre question, and it certainly offends conventional wisdom about what makes up a “healthy diet.” But a major six-month randomized controlled trial just published in a top science journal put versions of these diets head-to-head. Researchers compared: A low-carb, high-fat ketogenic diet (4% Calories from Carbs) A Mediterranean diet (50% Calories from Carbs) A low-fat plant-based diet (70% Calories from Carbs) This was unusually rigorous for a nutrition trial. Researchers recruited participants with obesity, provided them with all their meals, designed each diet to cause the same amount of weight loss, and followed them for six months. They performed a battery of metabolic assessments, including MRI and DEXA scans and advanced metabolic challenges you can’t just get at your average doctor’s clinic. And The Winner Is… And I’ll reveal the punchline to you: Across several important cardiometabolic outcomes, the low-carb, high-fat ketogenic diet won. All three diets caused similar amounts of weight loss (~10% weight loss). But the ketogenic diet produced greater reductions in: Liver fat Blood sugar Triglycerides (fat in the blood) Inflammation markers Insulin resistance scores The authors themselves concluded: “These results demonstrate that a very-low-carbohydrate diet has greater cardiometabolic benefits [as compared to a Mediterranean or very-low-fat diet] in people with metabolically unhealthy obesity.” Less Liver Synthesis of New Sugar and Fat You can also take a look at liver function.

title: GLP-1s May Change Cardiology Forever
description: A physician friend recently told me he had just taken a patient off a statin. Not because the patient’s cholesterol had plummeted. Not because they were experiencing side effects. Not because the patient refused treatment. Quite the opposite. The patient had become metabolically healthier. Healthy enough, in fact, that their physician concluded the statin was no longer providing a meaningful net benefit. If you’ve been told for years that elevated cholesterol automatically means lifelong statin therapy, that decision may sound strange, even reckless. It certainly goes against cardiology dogma to take a patient off a statin. But it follows directly from a reality that is often lost in public discussions of cardiovascular disease: The risk associated with LDL cholesterol (and ApoB) is context-dependent. For people with obesity, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, elevated triglycerides, low HDL, and other markers of metabolic dysfunction, statins can provide net benefit. This is for reasons beyond LDL and ApoB lowering, including improvements in endothelial function and reductions in vascular inflammation. That is… when a patient is metabolically unhealthy. But as metabolic health improves, the risk-benefit equation changes. Statins are not without costs. They can cause insulin resistance , impair mitochondrial function , and carry other side effects that become increasingly relevant as their expected benefits diminish. Even in the landmark trials that established statins as standard of care, when you examine participants with even modestly good metabolic health, the cardiovascular benefits become progressively smaller… and then become non-significant. The risks, meanwhile, remain.

title: The Science of Better Focus and Calmer Minds (Semax & Selank)
description: When I first heard about the peptides “ semax ” and “ selank ,” it was from a family friend who simply said: “ Since I started snorting these peptides, my mood has been the best it’s been in decades! ” Naturally, I was a little concerned. Hearing those words for the first time, they sounded like party drugs. And when a family friend discloses that they’ve been snorting [insert unknown compound here] and feeling on top of the world, that’s bound to raise a yellow flag. However, my concern turned to curiosity when I learned what these compounds actually were, and once I tried them myself. When I did — in the middle of an absolutely maddening homeowner nightmare — I noticed an abrupt shift toward calm and equanimity. I'll tell you that story shortly. But first, let's review the science. These peptides were first studied in Russia and are now used for certain medical indications, including stroke , as well as now recreationally to reduce anxiety and to improve focus and mental clarity. So today, we’re going to move beyond the sketchy names that sound either like party drugs ( or—in the case of semax—some strange manosphere supplement aimed at maximizing sperm quality ), and explore a scientific story grounded in some fascinating biology. What is Semax? Semax is, at its core, a fragment of the hormone adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). This is a hormone normally released by the pituitary gland that signals the adrenal glands to release hormones like cortisol.
